key_points.text: Write algorithms as flowcharts, pseudocode or program code (OCR pseudocode is used in questions; your syntax doesn't need to be perfect). There are usually several ways to solve a task, and they differ in execution time and memory; compare them for a given data set, and compare how one algorithm performs on different data sets.

Big O shows how time or space grows with input size n, keeping only the dominant term. From best to worst: constant O(1), logarithmic O(log n), linear O(n), polynomial O(n²) and higher, exponential O(2^n). Recognise and sketch each shape on a graph, and read and write the notation.
Best, average and worst cases differ because they depend on the data (for example, sorted, random or reversed). Learn these complexities:
key_points.code:
Algorithm        Best         Average      Worst
Linear search    O(1)         O(n)         O(n)
Binary search    O(1)         O(log n)     O(log n)
Bubble sort      O(n)         O(n²)        O(n²)
Insertion sort   O(n)         O(n²)        O(n²)
Merge sort       O(n log n)   O(n log n)   O(n log n)
Quick sort       O(n log n)   O(n log n)   O(n²)

key_points.text: Data structure algorithms: add to and remove from stacks, queues, trees and linked lists, including when built from a static array. Depth-first (post-order) traversal visits left subtree, right subtree, then the node (using recursion or a stack); breadth-first visits level by level using a queue. Recommend structures for scenarios (stack for undo, queue for buffers).
Linear search checks every item in turn: works on unsorted data, O(n). Binary search needs sorted data (a precondition) and halves the search area each step: O(log n), much faster on large data sets.
key_points.code:
function binarySearch(items, target)
    low = 0
    high = items.length - 1
    while low <= high
        mid = (low + high) DIV 2
        if items[mid] == target then
            return mid
        elseif items[mid] < target then
            low = mid + 1
        else
            high = mid - 1
        endif
    endwhile
    return -1
endfunction

key_points.text: Bubble sort swaps adjacent items that are out of order, pass after pass, stopping when a pass makes no swaps. Insertion sort inserts each item into its place in a growing sorted section. Both are simple and sort in place (little extra memory), fast on nearly sorted data, but O(n²) on average.
key_points.code:
procedure bubbleSort(items:byRef)
    do
        swapped = false
        for i = 0 to items.length - 2
            if items[i] > items[i + 1] then
                temp = items[i]
                items[i] = items[i + 1]
                items[i + 1] = temp
                swapped = true
            endif
        next i
    until swapped == false
endprocedure

key_points.text: Merge sort splits the list down to single items and merges them back in order: always O(n log n), but needs extra memory for the merged lists. Quick sort partitions round a pivot and sorts each side: usually O(n log n) and needs little extra memory, but O(n²) if the pivots are badly chosen (e.g. already sorted data with the first item as pivot).

Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest distance from a start node to all other nodes in a weighted graph: visit the unvisited node with the smallest distance, update its neighbours if a shorter route is found, repeat. A* finds the shortest path to one goal, choosing the node with the lowest cost so far plus a heuristic estimate to the goal; with a good heuristic that never overestimates, it finds the shortest path while exploring fewer nodes.

dont_confuse.text: Linear vs binary search: linear works on any data but checks items one by one; binary needs sorted data and halves the search area each time.
Bubble vs insertion sort: bubble sort swaps neighbours in repeated passes; insertion sort takes each item and slots it into a sorted section.

Merge vs quick sort: merge sort splits evenly and does the work when merging (always O(n log n), extra memory); quick sort does the work when partitioning round a pivot (O(n²) worst case, little extra memory).
Dijkstra vs A*: Dijkstra finds shortest paths to every node with no sense of direction; A* heads for one goal using a heuristic.
Depth-first vs breadth-first: depth-first goes deep down one branch first (stack or recursion); breadth-first goes level by level (queue).
Logarithmic vs exponential: O(log n) grows slower than linear; O(2^n) grows faster than any polynomial.
